parsed_answer.content:
When designing modern microservice architectures, choosing the right communication paradigm between gRPC and REST fundamentally dictates latency, developer ergonomics, network utilization, and client compatibility. REST (Representational State Transfer) has reigned supreme for decades as the web's standard architectural style, relying heavily on HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, resource-oriented URIs, and payload formats like JSON. While human-readable and universally supported by every web browser out of the box, REST suffers from textual payload overhead, loose runtime typing, and inefficient multiplexing when handling bidirectional asynchronous streams. Conversely, gRPC is a high-performance, open-source universal RPC framework developed by Google. It leverages HTTP/2 as its transport layer, Protocol Buffers (protobuf) as its interface definition and serialization mechanism, and natively supports four distinct communication patterns. Performance in gRPC is optimized through binary serialization which drastically shrinks payload size and eliminates expensive text-parsing CPU cycles on the JVM or other runtimes.

Type safety in gRPC is enforced strictly via `.proto` schema definitions. Developers compile these files into strongly-typed Java classes (or classes for any other language), completely eradicating entire classes of bugs related to JSON deserialization mismatches, missing fields, or unexpected null types. Streaming is another area where gRPC utterly diverges from standard REST; while REST relies on workarounds like Server-Sent Events (SSE) or WebSockets, gRPC provides native unary, client-streaming, server-streaming, and bidirectional-streaming out of the box, multiplexed over a single persistent TCP connection via HTTP/2 frames. However, browser support remains the primary Achilles' heel for gRPC. Because standard web browsers do not expose low-level HTTP/2 framing required to write gRPC clients directly, developers must deploy proxies like Envoy alongside the gRPC-Web specification to translate HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 JSON-to-protobuf traffic, introducing an extra infrastructure hop.

items: Protocol Buffers serialize data into compact binary formats using varints and tag-length-value structures, bypassing the severe string allocation overhead and garbage collection pressure caused by parsing massive JSON trees in Jackson or Gson.

HTTP/2 multiplexing allows multiple gRPC calls and streams to flow concurrently over a single TCP connection, eliminating the head-of-line blocking issues historically found in HTTP/1.1 REST environments.

gRPC-Web functions by wrapping binary gRPC payloads inside base64-encoded HTTP POST requests, requiring a specialized proxy to unpack and translate frames into standard HTTP/2 binary gRPC before reaching internal backend microservices.

parsed_answer.content: When implementing gRPC in a Spring Boot or cloud-native Java microservices ecosystem, watch out for connection pool exhaustion and load balancer configuration. Standard Layer 4 load balancers will pin a single gRPC bidirectional stream to one backend pod indefinitely because HTTP/2 keeps the underlying TCP socket open. You must utilize Layer 7 load balancing (like Envoy or Kubernetes ingress controllers supporting gRPC) to ensure proper request distribution across your pod replicas.

title: gRPC vs REST — performance, type safety, streaming, browser support
